title: Campaign Finance and Speech
short: Buckley v. Valeo (1976) upheld limits on contributions but struck down limits on independent expenditures; Citizens United v. FEC (2010), 5 to 4, held corporations and unions may spend independently on elections; disclosure rules have mostly been upheld.
trouble: Students think Buckley treated contributions and expenditures the same. It distinguished them: contribution limits survive more easily because of the risk of corruption.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

Running for office costs money: for ads, staff and travel. Laws that limit raising or spending money for elections therefore affect political speech, the speech the First Amendment protects most. Congress and the states have tried to limit money to prevent corruption, and the Court has drawn lines that both sides of the debate argue about. You met the basics in Civics: campaign finance.

opts.facts: After Watergate, Congress amended the Federal Election Campaign Act in 1974 to limit contributions to candidates, limit independent spending by others, limit candidates' spending of their own money, cap total campaign spending, and require disclosure.
opts.reasoning: The per curiam opinion said spending money on political communication is speech. Contribution limits were upheld: they serve the interest in preventing corruption and its appearance, and a contribution is a general expression of support, so a limit restricts the contributor's speech only marginally. Expenditure limits (independent spending, candidates' own funds, total campaign spending) were struck down: they directly restrict the quantity of political speech. Disclosure rules were largely upheld.

blocks.html: Thirty-four years later, Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (2010) held 5 to 4 that the government may not ban corporations and unions from spending their own money independently on election speech; it overruled Austin v. Michigan Chamber of Commerce (1990) and part of McConnell v. FEC (2003). The case began with a nonprofit corporation's film about a presidential candidate. By 8 to 1, the Court upheld the disclaimer and disclosure rules. McCutcheon v. FEC (2014) struck down aggregate limits on how much one donor could give to all candidates combined. The debate. Supporters of these rulings say that the First Amendment protects political speech whoever pays for it, that independent spending does not corrupt candidates, and that limits favor incumbents and the media. Critics, including the Citizens United dissent (Justice Stevens), say that large spending gives some voices outsized influence, that corporations are not people in the same sense, and that the appearance of corruption harms public trust. Both views are held by serious scholars and judges.

blocks.html: Buckley v. Valeo (1976) upheld contribution limits (anti-corruption interest) but struck down expenditure limits (direct limits on speech). Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (2010), 5 to 4, held corporations and unions may spend independently on elections; disclosure rules have mostly been upheld.

blocks.title: Which line?
blocks.q: A state caps how much a person may give directly to a governor's campaign at 2,000 dollars, and separately caps how much a person may spend on her own independent ads supporting the governor at 5,000 dollars. Which cap is vulnerable?
steps: The cap on contributions to the campaign fits Buckley's holding: it serves the anti-corruption interest.
The cap on independent spending limits the quantity of speech directly; Buckley struck such limits down.

blocks.title: Disclosure
blocks.q: After Citizens United, may Congress require an ad paid for by a corporation to say who paid for it?
steps: Citizens United, by 8 to 1, upheld disclaimer and disclosure requirements.
Disclosure burdens speech less and helps voters evaluate it.
blocks.a: Yes; disclaimers and disclosure were upheld.

blocks.html: Thinking Buckley treated contributions and expenditures the same. It distinguished them: contribution limits survive more easily because of the risk of corruption (a contribution goes to the candidate); limits on independent expenditures directly restrict speech and fell.
